rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God spoke after the preceding events out of concern to counsel Adam.
rows.anchor: عقيب ذلك اعتناء بنصح إدم عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preposition is repeated because, according to most grammarians, a preposition cannot coordinate directly onto a genitive pronoun without repetition.
rows.anchor: لأنه لايعطف على الضمير المجرور بدون إعادة الجار عند الجمهور

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some say the repeated lām stresses that Satan is intrinsically Eve’s enemy, not merely so through his enmity to Adam.
rows.anchor: للدلالة على أن عداوة اللعين للزوجة اصالة لاتبعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even if repeating the preposition is grammatically obligatory, that does not prevent it from serving the contextual emphasis proposed by Ibn Malik’s position.
rows.anchor: كون الشئ لازما بحسب القاعدة النحوية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling her Adam’s wife rather than naming Hawwa adds aversion to Satan and strengthens the warning.
rows.anchor: في التعبير بزوجك دون حواء من مزيد التنفير والتحذير

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: One explanation is that Satan’s enmity arose simply from envy; Satan and his followers were the first to envy.
rows.anchor: فقيل مجرد الحسد وهو لعنه الله تعالى ولعن اتباعه

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another explanation contrasts the old, ignorant Satan with the young, learned Adam; the ignorant are characteristically enemies of the learned.
rows.anchor: كونه شيخا جاهلا وكون آدم عليه السلام شابا عالما

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: A third explanation is the opposition of their origins: Satan was created from fire, Adam from clay, and Hawwa from Adam.
rows.anchor: فإن اللعين خلق من نار وآدم عليه السلام خلق من طين وحواء خلقت منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prohibition means they must not let Satan become the cause of their expulsion; it indirectly forbids placing themselves where he can expel them.
rows.anchor: فلا يكونن سببا لأخراجكما ( من الجنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The indirect prohibition is comparable to the address “let there be no constriction in your breast” in 7:2.
rows.anchor: فلا يكن في صدرك حرج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fāʾ orders the prohibition as a consequence of Satan’s enmity, or of being informed about that enmity.
rows.anchor: والفاء لترتيب موجب النهي على عداوته لهما أو على الأخبار بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hardship is the multitude of worldly travails, from which no one is spared; Adam alone is named because he is primary in household affairs and his toil entails his wife’s, while the wording also completes the cadence.
rows.anchor: وإسناد ذلك إليه عليه السلام خاصة بعد تعليق الإخراج الموجب له بهما معا

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some restrict the hardship to earning the means of livelihood, which they regard as men’s responsibility.
rows.anchor: وقيل : المراد بالشقاء التعب في تحصيل مبادى المعاش

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿid ibn Jubayr reports that after Adam was sent down he was told to work a piebald ox; wiping sweat, Adam recognized this as the promised toil, then blamed Hawwa. Transmitted by ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn ʿAsakir, and others; no grading is stated.
rows.anchor: عن سعيد ابن جبير قال : إن آدم عليه السلام لما اهبط من الجنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the livelihood reading has supporting material, al-Alusi finds it debatable and prefers the broader meaning of hardship.
rows.anchor: وكذا أيد بالآية بعد وفيه تأمل ولعل القول بالعموم أولى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb may be subjunctive with an understood an after the prohibition, or indicative as a new clause meaning “then you will suffer”; al-Alusi rejects the latter because the point is a consequence, not a prediction.
rows.anchor: تشقى ) يحتمل أن يكون منصوبا بإضمار أن في جواب النهي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase means the sun does not strike Adam; Arabic also uses ḍaḥā/ḍaḥiya for exposure to sunlight.
rows.anchor: ولاتصيبك الشمس يقال : ضحا كسى وضحى كرضى

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some explain the phrase as not being exposed to the sun; the author says this second usage is also established in Arabic.
rows.anchor: ويقال ضحا ضحوا وضحوا وضحيا إذا برز لها

rows.speaker: عمرو بن أبي ربيعة
rows.claim: A line by ʿAmr ibn Abi Rabiʿa uses yaḍḥā for exposure to the sun, while the person grows cold in the evening.
rows.anchor: رأت رجلا أيما إذا الشمس عارضت فيضحى وأما بالعشي فيخصر

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: The explanation that the sun does not strike him is transmitted from ʿIkrima.
rows.anchor: والتفسير الأول مروي عن عكرمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The four negations explain why the prohibition matters: the garden’s complete comforts make it vital to stay and avoid the cause of expulsion.
rows.anchor: والجملة تعليل لما يوجبه النهي فإن اجتماع أسباب الراحة فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Negating hunger, thirst, nakedness, and sun exposure recalls the feared afflictions more strongly than simply promising food, drink, clothing, and pleasant dwellings.
rows.anchor: والعدول عن التصريح بأن له عليه السلام فيها تنعما بفنون النعم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The negation means none of the four afflictions ever reaches him; he does not first suffer hunger and then obtain satiety, for example.
rows.anchor: أن لا يصيبه شئ من الأمور الأربعة اصلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The permission to enjoy everything in the garden except the tree already expressed the positive side of this promise, so it is omitted here.
rows.anchor: بما سوغ له من التمتع بجميع ما فيها سوى الشجرة

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: One report says Adam asked whether the garden had food, clothing, drink, and shade; God answered with these four assurances. Al-Alusi doubts the report’s authenticity.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم : أن الاقتصار على ما ذكر لما وقع في سؤال آدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adam is singled out here for the same reason given above; another suggestion is that he was the one who asked about these needs.
rows.anchor: ووجه افراده عليه السلام بما ذكر ما مر آنفا وقيل : كونه السائل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The arrangement pairs inner emptiness (hunger) with outer nakedness, then inner heat (thirst) with outer heat from the sun.
rows.anchor: وهي أن الجوع خلو الباطن والعرى خلو الظاهر

rows.speaker: الكشف
rows.claim: Al-Kashf says satiety and clothing are primary blessings, with drink and shade as complements, clarifying the favor; it also notes the distinction between inna laka and innaka.
rows.anchor: وفي الكشف إنما عدل إلى المنزل تنبيها على أن الشبع والكسوة أصلان

rows.speaker: الطيبي
rows.claim: Al-Tibi says the four items are ordered by importance, expand the warning about expulsion, and by repeating fīhā and the negation allude to worldly hardship, since the garden is only for delight.
rows.anchor: وفي تنسيق المذكورات الأربعة مرتبة هكذا مقدما ما هو الأهم

rows.speaker: الانتصاف
rows.claim: Al-Intisaf calls separating corresponding items qatʿ al-naẓīr ʿan al-naẓīr: separating each pair prevents two blessings seeming like one and emphasizes their number.
rows.anchor: وفي الانتصاف أن في الآية سرا بديعا من البلاغة يسمى قطع النظير عن النظير

rows.speaker: الكندي الأول
rows.claim: The first Kindi’s verse separates riding for pleasure from urging horses to wheel back, and a woman’s embrace from drinking, to multiply his pleasures and boasts.
rows.anchor: الكندي الأول : كأني لم اركب جوادا للذة

rows.speaker: الكندي الآخر
rows.claim: The later Kindi likewise separates passing heroes from his smiling face and bright teeth, following the same rhetorical device.
rows.anchor: الكندي الآخر فقال : وقفت وما في الموت شك

rows.speaker: سيف الدولة
rows.claim: Sayf al-Dawla reproached the later Kindi for separating corresponding items; the poet answered that by this standard Imruʾ al-Qays would also be at fault, citing the first Kindi’s lines.
rows.anchor: سيف الدولة إذ قطع الشئ عن نظيره فقال له : إن كنت أخطأت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi questions whether the Kindi’s lines actually separate corresponding things, since riding and urging horses both express bravery, while the woman and wine share pleasure.
rows.anchor: في بيتي الأول : إنه جمع بين ركوب الخيل للذة والنزهة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He questions whether cadence requires this exact order; claiming the sequence serves the rhyme assumes without proof that another order could not do so.
rows.anchor: قصد تناسب الفواصل في الآية ظاهر في أنه لو عدل عن هذا الترتيب

rows.speaker: شيبه ونافع وحفص وابن سعدان
rows.claim: Shayba, Nafiʿ, Hafs, and Ibn Saʿdan read innaka with a kasra; most readers read annaka with a fatḥa.
rows.anchor: شيبه ونافع وحفص وابن سعدان ( انك ) بكسر الهمزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With the majority’s fatḥa, the clause coordinates with an lā tajūʿa and becomes a verbal noun governed as the subject of inna; the two assertive particles do not conflict because they assert different relations.
rows.anchor: على أن العطف على أن لا تجوع وهو في تأويل مصدر اسم لأن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wāw is not an assertive particle, so it does not create two assertions in one domain; the meaning emphasizes assured freedom from thirst and sun exposure.
rows.anchor: حيث لم تكن حرفا موضوعا للتحقيق لم يلزم من دخولها اجتماع حر في التحقيق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi says the reason for emphasizing assured freedom from thirst and sun exposure, unlike the preceding clause, still needs explanation and invites reflection.
rows.anchor: بيان النكتة في عدم الاقتصار على بيان أن الثابت له عدم الظمأ

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: One says wāw stands for anna, but laka after it supplies a separator; al-Alusi calls this explanation plainly weak.
rows.anchor: وقيل إن الواو وإن كانت نائبة عن أن هنا إلا أنه يلاحظ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With the kasra reading, coordination is onto the first inna together with its clause, not just onto its subject.
rows.anchor: ولا يخفى عليك أن العطف على قراءة الكسر على أن الأولى مع معموليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement answers an implied question about what God commanded Adam after the preceding account.
rows.anchor: استئناف مبني على سؤال نشأ من الأخبار بأنه تعالى عامله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command tells Adam and his wife to descend together from the garden to earth.
rows.anchor: أي انزلا من الجنة إلى الأرض مجتمعين

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some take the dual address to be Adam and Iblis, since Iblis entered the garden to whisper after being expelled and declared accursed.
rows.anchor: وقيل : الخطاب له عليه السلام ولابليس عليه اللعنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the Adam-and-wife reading, enmity is between their descendants, since the two are ancestors from whom the children arise; the clause is circumstantial.
rows.anchor: لما أنهما أصل الذرية ومنشأ الأولاد فالتعادي في الحقيقة بين أولادهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the first reading, the enmity clause functions as a circumstantial clause describing their state as they descend.
rows.anchor: والجملة في موضع الحال أي متعادين في أمر المعاش وشهوات الأنفس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the addressees are Adam and Iblis, their own enmity and enmity between their descendants are evident.
rows.anchor: وعلى الثاني ظاهر لظهور العداوة بين آدم عليه السلام وإبليس

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some take the pronoun to encompass Adam and his descendants, and Iblis and his descendants.
rows.anchor: ومن هنا قيل : الضمير لآدم وذريته وابليس وذريته

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: A further proposal includes Adam, Iblis, the serpent, and their descendants; al-Alusi says the first interpretation is relied upon.
rows.anchor: وزعم بعضهم أن لآدم وإبليس والحية والمعول عليه الأول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The guidance is a prophet sent to the people and a book revealed to them.
rows.anchor: أي نبي أرسله إليكم وكتاب أنزله عليكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The explicit noun instead of a pronoun, attached to God, honors the guidance and intensifies the duty to follow it.
rows.anchor: وضع الظاهر موضع المضمر مع الإضافة إلى ضميره تعالى لتشريفه

words: فَمَنِ ٱتَّبَعَ هُدَاىَ فَلَا يَضِلُّ وَلَا يَشْقَىٰ
rows.speaker: أبو الطفيل
rows.claim: Al-Tabarani and others report from Abu al-Tufayl that the Prophet recited the clause with hudan indefinite, explaining that its follower does not stray in this life or suffer in the next; no grading is stated.
rows.anchor: وأخرج الطبراني وغيره عن أبي الطفيل أن النبي ( صلى الله عليه وسلم ) قرأ

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some identify guidance specifically as the Qur’an; Ibn Abbas said God protects its follower from worldly error and afterlife misery, then recited the verse.
rows.anchor: وفسر بعضهم الهدى بالقرآن لما أخرج ابن أبي شيبة وعبد بن حميد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas is also reported in a Prophetic report: whoever follows God’s Book, God guides him from error in this life and protects him from evil reckoning on Judgment Day; no grading is stated.
rows.anchor: وأخرج جماعة عنه مرفوعا إلى رسول الله ( صلى الله عليه وسلم ) بلفظ

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some favor taking guidance as the Qur’an because the next verse says “whoever turns away from My remembrance,” and the following account refers to God’s signs.
rows.anchor: ورجح على العموم بقيام القرينة عليه وهو قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi prefers the general meaning: dhikr can mean the Qur’an or any divine scripture, and signs can mean proofs generally.
rows.anchor: والمختار العموم أن يقول : الذكر يقع على القرآن وعلى سائر الكتب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhikr is also explained as guidance, since it causes remembrance of God and worship; the effect is named while the cause is intended.
rows.anchor: وقد فسر الذكر أيضا هنا بالهدى لأنه سبب ذكره تعالى وعبادته سبحانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report specifies the most honored instances encompassed by the general promise, highlighting their importance.
rows.anchor: وما في الخبر من باب التنصيص على حكم أشرف الأفراد المدلول عليه بالعموم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report’s interpretation—no error in this world and no suffering in the hereafter—is supported by transmitted reports.
rows.anchor: بقولنا في الدنيا ( ولا يشقى ) بقولنا في الآخرة هو الذي يقتضيه الخبر

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another reading reverses the domains: the guided person will not lose the way to Paradise in the hereafter or tire in securing livelihood in this world.
rows.anchor: وجوز بعضهم العكس أي فلا يضل طريق الجنة في الآخرة

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: On that reading, not straying in the hereafter answers the warning about resurrection blind, while not suffering in this life answers the constricted livelihood.
rows.anchor: وجعل الأول في مقابلة ( ونحشره يوم القيامة أعمى ) والثاني في مقابلة

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: The reversed order reflects the guided people’s focus on the afterlife, unlike those whose attention is confined to worldly life.
rows.anchor: وتقديم حال الآخرة على حال الدنيا في المهتدين لأن مطمح نظرهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi says reports support the first, worldly-error/afterlife-suffering interpretation; the reversed reading is attractive but somewhat strained.
rows.anchor: ولا يخفى أن الذي نطقت به الآثار هو الأول وذكر بعضهم أنه المتبادر

rows.speaker: الإمام
rows.claim: The Imam allows both consequences in the afterlife, or both in worldly life; on the latter reading there is no religious error or hardship caused by religion, though other hardship may occur.
rows.anchor: وجوز الإمام كون الأمرين في الآخرة وكونهما في الدنيا وذكر أن المراد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi says the interpretation supported by the reports remains the one to rely on.
rows.anchor: والمعول عليه ما سمعت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Turning away from remembrance means failing to follow it.
rows.anchor: والمراد من الاعراض عن الذكر عدم الاتباع فكانه قيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḍank means constricted and severe; as a verbal noun/adjective it describes masculine or feminine and any number, with feminine here following the noun’s original gender.
rows.anchor: أي ضيقة شديدة وهو مصدر ضنك وكذا ضناكة ولذا يوصف به المذكر والمؤنث

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan reads ḍankā with feminine alif and imāla, construing it as an adjective.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن ( ضنكى ) بألف التأنيث ككرى وبالامالة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses it as severe in every respect and cites a line describing a narrow, intensely confined pass.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس تفسيره بالشديد من كل وجه وأنشد قول الشاعر : والخيل قد لحقت بنا

rows.speaker: عطاء وابن جبير
rows.claim: The apparent meaning is a constricted life in this world; this interpretation is transmitted from ʿAta and Ibn Jubayr.
rows.anchor: والمتبادر أن تلك المعيشة له في الدنيا وروي ذلك عن عطاء وابن جبير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worldly life is constricted for the disbeliever because he is consumed by greed, acquisition, fear of loss, and miserliness, unlike the believer who seeks the afterlife.
rows.anchor: ووجه ضيق معيشة الكافر المعرض في الدنيا أنه شديد الحرص على الدنيا

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another explanation takes ḍank as a life without good, a burden for the disbeliever and added punishment on Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: وقيل : الضنك حجاز عما لا خير فيه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says wealth given to a servant who does not fear God in its use has no good and is constricted livelihood; Ibn Abi Hatim transmits this gloss.
rows.anchor: مما أخرجه ابن أبي حاتم عن ابن عباس أنه قال في الآية : يقول كل مال

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some say this life is called constricted because it causes constriction on Judgment Day, naming the cause by its effect; reports from ʿIkrima and Malik ibn Dinar point this way.
rows.anchor: وقيل : المراد من كونها ضنكا إنها سبب للضنك يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود وأبو سعيد الخدري وأبو صالح والربيع والسدي ومجاهد
rows.claim: These early authorities interpret the constricted life as punishment in the grave.
rows.anchor: عن ابن مسعود وأبي سعيد الخدري وأبي صالح والربيع والسدي ومجاهد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Bahr transmits from Ibn Abbas that the verse concerned al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd al-Asad al-Makhzumi and means the grave’s crushing pressure until his ribs diverge; it is also reported as Prophetic.
rows.anchor: وفي البحر عن ابن عباس أن الآية نزلت في الأسود بن عبد الأسد المخزومي

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: Abu Hurayra reports the Prophet saying the believer’s grave is spacious and luminous, while the verse refers to the unbeliever’s grave punishment by ninety-nine multiheaded serpents until resurrection; no grading is stated.
rows.anchor: عن أبي هريرة قال قال رسول الله ( صلى الله عليه وسلم ) المؤمن في قبره

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد
rows.claim: Abu Saʿid reports the Prophet interpreting the constricted life as grave punishment; one wording says the grave narrows until the ribs diverge, another calls it the grave’s squeeze. No grading is stated.
rows.anchor: عن أبي سعيد قال : قال رسول الله ( صلى الله عليه وسلم ) في قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Those who place the constricted life before the great Resurrection count what happens after death as part of worldly life.
rows.anchor: ومن قال : الدنيا ماقبل القيامة الكبرى قال : مايكون بعد الموت

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Another view places the constricted life in Hell on Judgment Day; al-Hasan’s view is transmitted by Ibn Abi Shayba and Ibn al-Mundhir.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم : إنها تكون يوم القيامة في جهنم وأخرج ذلك ابن أبي شيبة

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says the Hellish livelihood consists of thorns, zaqqum, ghislin, and darīʿ, and that livelihood exists only in the afterlife.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن أبي حاتم عن ابن زيد قال : المعيشة الضنك في النار شوك وزقوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If grave reports are sound, al-Alusi says their meaning must be followed; if not, the worldly-life reading is preferable because the resurrection clause follows.
rows.anchor: وإن لم تصح كان الأولى القول بأنها في الدنيا لا في الآخرة

rows.speaker: أبان بن تغلب
rows.claim: A group including Aban ibn Taghlib reads the r of wa-naḥshuruhu as quiescent, as lightening or as a jussive coordinated with the conditional answer fa-inna lahu.
rows.anchor: وقرأت فرقة منهم أبان بن تغلب ( ونحشره ) بإسكان الراء

rows.speaker: أبان بن تغلب
rows.claim: Ibn Khalawayh attributes to Aban a reading with quiescent hā, treating connected speech like a pause; al-Bahr prefers the dialect of Banu Kilab and ʿUqayl, who quiesce such pronouns.
rows.anchor: ونقل ابن خالويه عن أبان أنه قرأ ( ونحشره ) بسكون الهاء

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: Another group reads yaḥshuruhu with yāʾ rather than naḥshuruhu with nūn.
rows.anchor: وقرأت فرقة ( ويحشره ) بالباء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent meaning of blind is lacking physical sight, as in the passage describing people gathered blind, mute, and deaf.
rows.anchor: الظاهر أن المراد فاقد البصر كما في قوله تعالى ( ونحشره يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As before, “he said” begins a new statement after an implied question arising from the preceding account.
rows.anchor: استئناف كما مر ( رب لم حشرتني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The contrast is with the person’s sight in worldly life; most rejecters had sight, though some were blind from birth.
rows.anchor: أي في الدنيا كما هو ظاهر ولعل هذا باعتبار أكثر أفراد من أعرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question asks what sin earned this punishment; the person is either ignorant of the cause or assumes he committed no deserving sin.
rows.anchor: عن السبب الذي استحق به الحشر لأعمى لأنه جهل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi treats the kāf as extra, as in mithluka lā yabkhal; dhālika points to the manner of arrival, so the clear signs came to the person in that striking way.
rows.anchor: الكاف مقحمة كما في مثلك لا يبخل وذلك إشارة إلى مصدر أتتك

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari does not treat the kāf as extra: dhālika points to the person’s being resurrected blind, just as he acted, so he is treated accordingly.
rows.anchor: وعند الزمخشري لا إقحام وذلك إشارة إلى حشرة أعمى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s statement answers the implied question “What did I do?”: the signs came to the person, but he forgot them.
rows.anchor: جواب سؤال مقدر كأنه قيل : يا رب ما فعلت أنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Forgetting means abandoning the signs as if wholly forgotten, or becoming blind to them; the effect (forgetting) is named for its cause (turning away).
rows.anchor: أي تركتها ترك المنسي الذي لايذكر اصلا والمراد فعميت عنها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second dhālika points to the neglect implied by nasiya, and the kāf keeps its ordinary sense: as the person neglected the signs in life, he is left in blindness today as fitting recompense.
rows.anchor: النسيان المفهوم من نسيتها والكاف على ظاهرها

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some take the kāf as meaning “because of,” like the proposed reading of “remember Him as He guided you” in 2:198.
rows.anchor: وقيل : الكاف بمعنى اللام إلا جلية كما قيل في قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The abandonment continues until God removes the blindness and the person sees Judgment Day’s terrors and the Fire, becoming punishment upon punishment.
rows.anchor: ثم يزال العمى عنه فيرى أهوال القيامة ويشاهد النار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi links later sight of the Fire to the verse saying criminals see it and realize they will fall into it.
rows.anchor: كما قال سبحانه ( ورأى المجرمون النار فظنوا أنهم مواقعوها )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The blindness and deafness are later removed, as indicated by the verse “How clearly they will hear and see on the day they come to Us.”
rows.anchor: وكذا اليكم والصمم يزيلهما الله تعالى عنهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report from Ibn Abbas says the unbeliever is first resurrected seeing and then blinded; thus “I had been seeing” describes the beginning of resurrection. Al-Alusi says blindness apparently is later removed too.
rows.anchor: وفي رواية عن ابن عباس رضي الله تعالى عنه أن الكافر يحشر أولا بصيرا ثم يعمى

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: ʿIkrima says the person sees nothing except the Fire; al-Alusi suggests this may apply only at some point that Day, since otherwise the person could not read his record.
rows.anchor: وعن عكرمة أنه لايى شئ إلا النار

rows.speaker: مجاهد ومقاتل والضحاك وأبو صالح وابن عباس
rows.claim: These authorities, in one report from Ibn Abbas, take blindness as lack of proof or insight, and “I had been seeing” as knowing God’s proof and being able to argue in worldly life; Ibrahim ibn ʿUrfa chose this reading.
rows.anchor: وروي عن مجاهد ومقاتل والضحاك وأبي صالح هي رواية عن ابن عباس أيضا

rows.speaker: إبراهيم ابن عرفة
rows.claim: Ibrahim ibn ʿUrfa supports the insight reading with 22:46: the eyes are not blind, but the hearts within the chests are blind.
rows.anchor: واختار ذلك إبراهيم ابن عرفة وقال كلما ذكر الله سبحانه في كتابه العمى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the insight reading, God says the person was made blind to the argument that could aid him because he abandoned the proofs; as he left them in life, he is left blind forever.
rows.anchor: وحاصل الجواب علية إني حشرتك أعمى القلب لاتهتدي إلى ما يناجيك

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another explanation is that the person is bewildered, unable to devise ways to ward off punishment, like a blind person confused by what he cannot see.
rows.anchor: وقيل : المراد بأعمى متحيرا لايدري مايصنع من الحيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse does not prove that merely forgetting the Qur’an or one verse is a major sin: if signs include Qur’anic verses, “forgetting” here means abandoning them and not believing them.
rows.anchor: وليس في الآية دليل كما يتوهم على عد نسيان القرآن أو آية

rows.speaker: الرافعي
rows.claim: Al-Rafiʿi counts forgetting the Qur’an or a verse as a major sin; al-Alusi says al-Nawawi’s wording in al-Rawda seems to favor that view.
rows.anchor: كما ذهب إليه الإمام الرافعي ويشعر كلام الإمام النوري في الروضة

rows.speaker: أبو شامة
rows.claim: Abu Shama interprets traditions condemning forgetfulness of Qur’anic material as condemning failure to act on it; those counting literal forgetting major condition it on laziness and disregard, as al-Balqini and al-Zarkashi explain.
rows.anchor: نعم تجوز أبو شامة شيخ النووي فحمل النسيان في الأحاديث الواردة

rows.speaker: حمزة والكسائي وخلف
rows.claim: Hamza, al-Kisaʾi, and Khalaf use imala on both occurrences of aʿmā because it is a defective-yāʾ form.
rows.anchor: وقرأ حمزة والكسائي وخلف ( أعمى ) بالإمالة في الموضعين لأنه من ذوات الياء

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Abu ʿAmr uses imala at the first occurrence only, because it is an especially changeable verse ending and stopping point.
rows.anchor: وأمال أبو عمرو في الأول فقط لكونه جديرا بالتغيير لكونه رأس الآية ومحل الوقف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The punishment is like-for-like with the offense: God punishes those who plunge into desires and disbelieve in, deny, or turn away from their Lord’s signs.
rows.anchor: ومثل ذلك الجزاء الموافق للجناية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The general class of punishment is compared with the specific punishment just described.
rows.anchor: والمراد تشبيه الجزاء العام بالجزاء الخاص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hereafter’s punishment may mean punishment generally or specifically the Fire; it is harsher than the first punishment and lasts longer, or is harsher and more lasting than it, grave punishment, or resurrection blind.
rows.anchor: على الاطلاق أو عذاب النار
